First, a code node checks the three exact infeasibility conditions: an unknown predecessor, a precedence cycle (Kahn's algorithm), and a job with no mode whose requirements all name known resources within their maximum capacity. If any holds, it returns "infeasible". Otherwise a serial schedule-generation scheme decodes a priority vector, which is a random key per job plus an optional forced mode per job, into a valid schedule. Each job's resources are booked on per-time free-capacity arrays built from the calendars, and the search uses jump-ahead to find the earliest window that fits. When a job's mode is not forced, the decoder picks the mode that minimises finish time plus weighted tardiness. The search starts from several priority rules (due-adjusted latest finish, critical-path latest finish, earliest start, slack, and successor count). It then runs a time-budgeted local search that perturbs keys, swaps keys, changes modes, and re-decodes with the current start times as keys, keeping the best cost until about 0.7 s of CPU time.

The pipeline is one deterministic code node; it uses no LLM calls. Otherwise it builds per-time capacity arrays from the calendars and uses a serial schedule-generation scheme, which places each job at the earliest start where every resource fits in every period of its run. Its moves are precedence-respecting job shifts and mode flips, and the best valid schedule found is returned. change:
DIAGNOSIS: The weakest instances lose almost all their cost to weighted tardiness, not makespan. The current program cannot target that, for three reasons:
- **Priority lists ignore inherited urgency.** They are built from static keys (tail length, own-due slack). A job with no due date that precedes a heavily weighted, tightly due job gets no urgency, and weights are never compared against processing times.
- **Mode choice is myopic.** It minimises the job's own finish and tardiness, so it grabs fast, resource-heavy modes that block later work, and it ignores what that delay does to successors.
- **The search is too weak to recover.** Annealing moves jobs at random positions, so it rarely pulls the cause of a large tardiness earlier. With only a few hundred decodes per second, that cannot fix a poor start. I add a precomputed "effective urgency" layer:
- **Effective due dates** are propagated backward through successors, so each job inherits the earliest deadline it must meet for its weighted descendants.
- **Inherited weights** add up the weights of all due-dated descendants, using descendant bitsets.

  - The dynamic ATC-style constructive SGS with incremental start-time caching and randomised parameters. X was clearly stronger on the big and calendar_heavy families.

- **New:**
  - **Checkpointed incremental decoding.** The decoder saves the capacity profile and the running cost every few list positions. A neighbour that changes the list or a mode at position p only re-decodes from the last checkpoint at or before p. This roughly doubles the number of SA evaluations, which matters most on big instances.
  - **Weighted choice of tardy jobs.** The job to pull earlier is drawn in proportion to w·tardiness, not uniformly.
  - **Due-date-aimed insertion.** A pulled job is moved to the list position whose start time matches its latest on-time start, not to a random position.

Due dates only affect the priority of the due-dated job itself, so its untimed predecessors get no urgency at all. The annealing then moves random jobs to random positions, so it rarely makes the one move that matters: pulling a tardy job and its whole predecessor chain forward. Every candidate is also decoded from scratch over the full horizon, which leaves only a few hundred evaluations within budget on big instances. There are three changes. First, deadlines are propagated backwards through the precedence graph, so predecessors inherit urgency, and the starting priority lists and random samples use these propagated deadlines. Second, the decoder now saves the partial schedule (capacity left, starts, modes, finishes) at checkpoints every B positions of the job list. A candidate list is re-decoded only from the first position that changed, which allows many more evaluations within the time limit. strategy: PARADIGM: Schedule-space Large Neighbourhood Search (time-window destroy & bounded re-insertion) with forward-backward justification. The search works directly on a concrete timetable: start times, modes and a live residual-capacity profile per resource, instead of on a priority list. Each move removes a coherent group of jobs: a start-time window, a cluster grown backwards from a tardy or makespan-critical job through predecessors and overlapping competitors, or a random set. It then re-inserts them into the holes left among the fixed jobs, choosing mode and time jointly. Each job's window is bounded by its fixed predecessors' finishes and its fixed successors' starts, so only the touched jobs are re-timed. Moves are accepted with annealing on the true cost. A monotone left-shift compaction pass and a forward-backward (right-justify then left-justify) pass run periodically. An exact feasibility check comes first, and the final schedule is verified independently, with a guaranteed-valid sequential fallback.

strategy: PARADIGM: Lagrangian price-coordinated decomposition (subgradient dual pricing of resource-time slots plus primal repair). The resource capacity constraints are relaxed and replaced by a price for every (resource, time) slot. Each iteration, every job independently picks its own cost-optimal (start, mode) in topological order, using price prefix sums. A job's cost is the prices of the slots it uses, its effective-due-date tardiness with inherited weights, and a soft makespan-target penalty. Prices then move by subgradient steps on the resulting overload and underuse, so contested windows become expensive and jobs spread themselves out. Each relaxed solution is turned into a feasible schedule by an eligibility-respecting serial decoder, keyed by the relaxed starts, once with the relaxed modes and once with greedy modes; the best one is kept. Any time left over is spent on a small key-jitter refinement around the best dual-derived ordering. Infeasibility is checked exactly as the spec defines it.

PARADIGM: Bounded-width beam search over the schedule-construction tree, guided by lower bounds. The program first checks feasibility exactly as the spec defines it: unknown predecessors, a precedence cycle (Kahn's algorithm), or a job with no mode that fits known resources at maximum capacity. Otherwise it explores many partial schedules in parallel. Each beam node holds its own residual-capacity profile and cached earliest feasible starts for every eligible (job, mode) pair; a placement only invalidates cached starts whose interval and resources overlap it. Children are first filtered by a cheap latest-start / start-delay rule. The survivors are then ranked by a lower bound on total cost: tardiness already locked in, plus tardiness and critical-path bounds on unscheduled jobs built from true resource-aware earliest finishes of the eligible frontier, plus a resource-energy bound on makespan. Width doubles over repeated runs, with varied ranking parameters and identical partial schedules removed, until the CPU-time budget runs out; the best complete schedule is returned.
